column63:
For me, while practical implications are also useful, it is most important to get a sufficient understanding of the research finding/method. However, I'm not interested in the methods section itself because that tends to provide technical details that don't meaningfully contribute to understanding of the topic (e.g. specific volumes of reagents used, the exact analysis software, etc.).

To give an example, after the first sentence of Summary #1 ("Immune checkpoint drugs help the immune system attack many types of cancer, but they can also harm healthy organs."), I wish it explained how immune checkpoint drugs actually work and then connected that mechanism to immune‑related side effects. Similarly, in Summary #7, I wished it could have described the method with more specificity as opposed to the vague labels of "tiny chemical marks on cell messages" or "message mark proteins." Avoiding jargon is definitely important, but perhaps at a point this avoidance comes at the cost of explanation quality. (Though, these were the only two instances I found the text too vague; the other summaries were excellent and clear.)

Usually, researchers would write a summary themselves to provide prospective participants needed context. In that case, I would prefer the human-made one to an AI-generated one. For example, a previous project I contributed to gave participants a "contract" that included all the details they would need to know about the study. In that case, an AI-generated lay-summary would not provide additional value. 

However, if the researchers requesting enrollment were not going to provide a summary themselves, then the inclusion of an AI-generated lay-summary would be helpful to improve my understanding of the task.

Yes, there were a few minor inaccuracies or potentially misleading simplifications, although the summaries were generally accurate.

For example, in the radioactive iodine refractory thyroid cancer study (Paper #4), the summary described the condition as cancer that "stops responding" to radioactive iodine. However, some patients may never demonstrate radioactive iodine uptake in the first place.

In the Mutographs study (Paper #2), the full-text summary suggested that whole-genome sequencing had already been completed for over 4,000 cases, whereas the abstract indicated that sequencing was still being finalized.

Overall, these issues did not substantially distort the main findings, but they highlight the importance of verifying AI-generated summaries against the original scientific publications.
